learn: What NLP is, where it comes from and where it is used
The levels of language analysis from morphology to pragmatics
Why language is hard: ambiguity at every level, plus idioms, non-standard text and world knowledge
The preprocessing pipeline: segmentation, tokenisation, stop words, stemming and lemmatisation
How to evaluate NLP systems, and the standard toolkits
intro.why: Every later topic (word vectors, language models, tagging, parsing, Transformers, retrieval and summarisation) is a way of handling the difficulties introduced here, and almost every pipeline starts with the preprocessing steps described in this session.

sections.title: What NLP is and where it is used
sections.plain: Getting computers to analyse, understand and generate human language.
sections.body:
Natural language processing (NLP) is the field that gets computers to analyse, understand and generate human languages, making the computer learn our language rather than us learning its. It began as a branch of artificial intelligence and draws on linguistics, psycholinguistics, cognitive science and statistics.

Most human knowledge lives in text (emails, web pages, articles, contracts, court decisions), and it grows daily; NLP is what lets machines read, search, translate and reason over it. Everyday applications: predictive text, spelling and grammar correction, search engines, voice assistants, spam filters, machine translation, question answering, text categorisation, sentiment analysis, information extraction and summarisation. Market estimates grew from about $15.7 billion (2022) toward $49.4 billion projected for 2027.

sections.title: Levels of language analysis
sections.plain: From word parts to grammar to meaning to context; each level constrains the next.
sections.body:
• Morphology: smallest meaningful units (morphemes): "fire" + "house"; the "-s" in "runs".
  • Lexical analysis: words and phrases (the lexicon); splitting text into words. "friendship" is valid, "friendful" is not.
  • Syntactic analysis: grammatical structure. "the girl goes to school" vs *"the girl go to the school".
  • Semantic analysis: literal meaning. "Colourless green ideas sleep furiously" is grammatical but meaningless.
  • Discourse integration: meaning across sentences ("She wanted it": who and what depend on earlier sentences).
  • Pragmatic analysis: meaning in situation ("Close the window" is a request).

Worked: three ways to be wrong. "Green frogs have large noses": syntactically and semantically fine, pragmatically odd. "Green ideas have large noses": grammatical, but broken semantically and pragmatically. "Large have green ideas nose": ungrammatical, so it fails at all three levels. A sentence can be correct low down yet wrong higher up.

sections.title: Understanding vs generation
sections.plain: Reading language in, versus deciding what to say and how to say it.
sections.body: Natural language understanding (NLU) analyses input across the levels above: from characters and words to structure, meaning and intent. Natural language generation (NLG) works in the other direction: planning (deciding what to say: content selection and organisation) and realisation (how to say it: syntactic generation, word choice, morphology). Many systems do both (dialogue, translation, summarisation).

sections.title: Ambiguity at every level
sections.plain: The same string can mean different things, and choosing correctly needs meaning and knowledge.
sections.body:
• Lexical: one word, several senses. "I saw bats": mammals or baseball bats?
  • Structural: one sentence, several parses. "Visiting relatives can be a nuisance" (visiting them, or relatives who visit?). "The professor said on Monday he would give an exam" (when was it said, or when is the exam?). "I saw the man with the telescope" (who has it?).
  • Headlines: "Teacher strikes idle kids": a teacher hitting idle kids, or teachers' strikes making kids idle?

Each reading is grammatical; choosing the intended one requires meaning and world knowledge, which is why NLP cannot be done by hand-written rules alone and leans on statistics and learned knowledge.

sections.title: Idioms, non-standard text and world knowledge
sections.plain: Beyond ambiguity: slang, word boundaries, figurative phrases, background knowledge and tricky names.
sections.body:
• Non-standard English: "gm", "gudnit", emoji, hashtags.
  • Segmentation issues: "The old city-bus stop": which words group together?
  • Idioms: "dark horse", "lose face": not literal.
  • World knowledge: "Mary and Sue are sisters" (sisters of each other) vs "Mary and Sue are mothers" (not of each other).
  • Tricky entity names: "Let It Be was recorded…", "Where is A Bug's Life playing?": titles that look like ordinary phrases.

sections.title: Preprocessing: segmentation, tokenisation, stop words
sections.plain: Clean raw text and cut it into sentences and tokens before any analysis.
sections.body:
• Sentence segmentation: split a paragraph into sentences, mostly at ".", "!", "?", but "." is ambiguous ("Dr.", "3.14", "U.S.").
  • Tokenisation: split a sentence into tokens (words, numbers, punctuation): "Asha offers corporate training." → [Asha, offers, corporate, training, .]. Modern models use subword tokens (M8, M11).
  • Stop-word removal: drop very common, low-information words ("the", "is", "a") for some tasks (search, topic models), but not for tasks where they matter ("not", word order in parsing).

Code example ex1 implements these steps from scratch on "Dr. Rao paid 3.14 dollars for coffee. She ran to the station! …", keeping "Dr." and "3.14" inside their sentence.

sections.title: Stemming vs lemmatisation
sections.plain: Chop suffixes quickly, or look up the true dictionary form.
sections.body:
Stemming strips affixes with rules to a crude stem: "running" → "run", "studies" → "studi" (a non-word). Fast and blunt (Porter stemmer).

Lemmatisation maps a word to its dictionary lemma using vocabulary, morphology and part of speech: "better" → "good", "ran" → "run", "studies" → "study". Smarter but slower and needs resources (e.g. WordNet).

Choose stemming for speed (search indexing), lemmatisation for correctness (analysis, generation, linguistically informed features).

sections.title: Context-free grammars and parse ambiguity
sections.plain: Rules that nest phrases inside phrases generate trees; one sentence can have several valid trees.
sections.body:
Most syntactic representations rest on context-free grammars: rules for how phrases combine plus a lexicon of word categories; a derivation is drawn as a parse tree.

$$S \to NP\ VP;\quad NP \to N\ N \mid N;\quad VP \to V\ NP \mid V\ PP;\quad PP \to P\ NP$$

Lexicon: rice: N; flies: N, V; like: V, P; sand: N.

Worked. "Rice flies like sand": (1) NP "rice flies" (N N) + VP "like sand" (V NP): rice-flies (insects) like sand; (2) NP "rice" + VP "flies like sand" (V PP): rice flies through the air as sand does. Same words, two valid trees: structural ambiguity made concrete. Code example ex2 enumerates exactly these two parses.

sections.title: Evaluating NLP systems; toolkits
sections.plain: Measure with metrics that fit the task, on a representative test set.
sections.body:
Classification-style tasks use a contingency table (true/false positives/negatives) and derived metrics: accuracy $(TP+TN)/N$, precision $TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $TP/(TP+FN)$, $F_1 = 2PR/(P+R)$. Example (ex2): TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 5, TN = 45 → accuracy 0.85, precision 0.80, recall 0.889, F1 0.842.

Key questions: which metric fits the task (accuracy misleads on imbalanced data); how to score open-ended outputs such as translations or summaries with many correct forms (BLEU, ROUGE, human judgement); whether human judgements are reliable (agreement); whether the test sample is representative.

Toolkits: NLTK (the classic Python toolkit), spaCy, Gensim, Stanford CoreNLP, Hugging Face Transformers; commercial APIs (IBM Watson, Google Cloud Natural Language, Amazon Comprehend).

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Rules vs statistics vs neural. Early NLP was rule-based; statistical NLP learned from corpora; neural NLP learns representations end to end. Modern systems still use rules for normalisation and safety.
  • Tokenisation is not neutral: subword tokenisers (BPE, WordPiece) split rare words into pieces, which affects cost and behaviour of language models across languages.
  • Language diversity: many techniques were developed for English; morphology-rich and low-resource languages need different preprocessing.
  • Evaluation leakage: test data that overlaps training data inflates scores; always check.

code.title: A preprocessing pipeline from scratch
code.explain: Segments sentences while protecting abbreviations and decimals, tokenises with a regular expression, removes stop words, and compares crude suffix stemming with dictionary lemmatisation.
mistakes: Splitting sentences at every full stop.
Removing stop words like 'not' before sentiment analysis.
code.notes: Real systems use trained segmenters/tokenisers (spaCy, NLTK punkt) and WordNet-based lemmatisers.
code.output:
sentence 1: Dr. Rao paid 3.14 dollars for coffee.
   tokens:       ['Dr', '.', 'Rao', 'paid', '3.14', 'dollars', 'for', 'coffee', '.']
   no stopwords: ['Dr', 'Rao', 'paid', 'dollars', 'coffee']
   stems:        ['dr', 'rao', 'paid', 'dollar', 'coffee']
   lemmas:       ['dr', 'rao', 'pay', 'dollar', 'coffee']
sentence 2: She ran to the station!
   tokens:       ['She', 'ran', 'to', 'the', 'station', '!']
   no stopwords: ['ran', 'station']
   stems:        ['ran', 'station']
   lemmas:       ['run', 'station']
sentence 3: The studies were better than expected; the children's toys are running out.
   tokens:       ['The', 'studies', 'were', 'better', 'than', 'expected', ';', 'the', "children's", 'toys', 'are', 'running', 'out', '.']
   no stopwords: ['studies', 'better', 'expected', "children's", 'toys', 'running']
   stems:        ['studi', 'better', 'expect', "children'", 'toy', 'run']
   lemmas:       ['study', 'good', 'expect', 'child', 'toy', 'run']

Note 'studies' -> stem 'studi' (not a word) but lemma 'study'; 'better' -> lemma 'good' needs a dictionary.

code.title: Enumerating parses with a tiny CFG, and evaluation metrics
code.explain: Exhaustively derives every parse of 'rice flies like sand' under the session's grammar (two trees), then computes accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from a contingency table.
mistakes: Assuming a grammar yields one parse per sentence.
code.notes: Exhaustive enumeration explodes for long sentences; chart parsing (M9) avoids it.
code.output:
'Rice flies like sand' has 2 parses:
   (S (NP (N rice)) (VP (V flies) (PP (P like) (NP (N sand)))))
   (S (NP (N rice) (N flies)) (VP (V like) (NP (N sand))))

TP=40 FP=10 FN=5 TN=45: accuracy 0.85, precision 0.80, recall 0.889, F1 0.842
If only 5 of 100 emails were spam, predicting 'not spam' always would score 95% accuracy with 0 recall.
